messages.body_plain:
Hi Pavel,

Thanks, I think you *may* be on the right track. If I rename the edge 
attributes as suggested, the estimation in the new statnet version runs 
considerably faster and shows much smaller log-likelihood improvements. 
The results are also closer to the original results. However, they are 
still not *very* close to the original results, with some of the 
estimates deviating significantly from the original estimates (in 
particular edges and gwesp but fortunately not the covariates).

I also re-ran the adjusted model 2 on the machine where the old package 
was installed, and the results didn't change compared to the published 
paper. I will paste the output of the estimation below. I don't remember 
exactly which version I was using in the paper (probably something close 
to 2.4 but not exactly 2.4), so the estimates below (produced using 
version 2.4) show some very small deviation from the AJPS version, but 
nothing to worry about. They are still different from the adjusted model 
2 estimates using the new ergm version though. You can also see that the 
names would *not* have ended up being identical in version 2.4, no 
matter if I renamed them or not.

The bottom line is that renaming doesn't change the results for version 
2.4, but it does change the results for version 3.1-0. In spite of the 
improvement, the adjusted model in the new ergm version still shows some 
deviations from the original results (but apparently much less severe 
than before).

Take care,

Philip

If your goal is to convert dutchdata[,46] into numeric values, maybe it 
would work to wrap it in a call to as.numeric:

as.numeric(as.factor(dutchdata[,46]))

best,
  -skye

On Thu, 6 Aug 2009, Jenine Harris wrote: 


> I was wondering if anyone has an example of how a GWDSP term would be 

> interpreted in somewhat lay terms. From my understanding GWDSP accounts for 

> the distribution of shared partnership for each dyad in a network, but I'm 

> not sure how to go about interpreting a negative signficant GWDSP 

> coefficient of -0.25 in an actual ERGM model. What does this say about the 

> distribution and how does it influence the likelihood of a tie? 



Hi Jenine, 

A great question. Yes, I do think GWDSP is a bit trickier than interpret 
than any of the other terms we commonly work with. I can give you my own 
idiosyncratic approach. 

First, as technical background: As you probably know, GWDSP is a 
parametric summary measure of the tendency for two actors to have x 
partners in common, regardless of whether the two actors themselves are 
tied. GWESP is the same measure, but only counted across two actors who 
are tied. The two are comparable to the "alternating 2-paths" and 
"alternating k-triangles" that Snijders et al discuss in a series of 
papers. The two measures, combined with a third (GW degree, or the 
comparable alternating k-stars) are derived in those papers by placing a 
parametric constraint on three sets of statistics that emerge when making 
a very sociologically reasonable set of assumptions about relational 
dependence. The three parametric stats are also seen to work well in 
practice at modeling real-world social networks and avoiding degeneracy 
when doing so. 

So, on to interpretation. As I said, I agree that GWDSP is the hardest to 
interpret. In fact, I personally never use a GWDSP term without also 
using a GWESP term. And once I combined the two, I always find that the 
GWDSP coefficient is close to zero, and non-significant. Let me see if I 
can give good intuition as to why. 

GWESP has some relatively clear interpetations (which I discuss in a few 
of my papers). In real-world data of friendship or collaboration or 
similar kinds of networks, it is generally significantly positive. This 
means that those who are tied are more likely than chance to have multiple 
shared partners. 

GWDSP tells whether shared partners tend to clump together, regardless of 
whether two people are tied or not. For example, whether or not you and I 
are friends, if we have one friend in common, are we more likely than 
expected by chance to have a second friend in common? And so on. If yes, 
the GWDSP coefficient will be positive. If it is zero, then we are as 
likely as chance to have one in common; if negative, then less. 

If one only uses GWDSP and not GWESP, then it's hard to know whether an 
observed non-random shared partner distribution is driven by pairs who are 
themselves tied, pairs who are not tied, or both. If you include both 
GWESP and GWDSP, then it becomes clear - GWDSP is the base effect (which 
now isolates the effect for those not tied only); GWESP occurs on top of 
this base, and isolates the effect for those who are tied. And what I 
have always found is that the GWESP effect is then strong and significant, 
and the GWDSP is tiny and insignificant. It may be that in different 
kinds of data GWDSP would be significant itself, though. 

My questions for you are: is your GWDSP term significant? Does it remain 
so when GWESP is added? If the answer to both questions is yes, then you 
have something particuarly interesting (and unprecendented, at least for 
me) on your hands. If it remains negative and significant, then that says 
that people who are not tied tend not to have multiple shared partners. 
Once two unconnected people have one shared partner, they're less likely 
than chance to have a second; if they do have a second, they're less 
likely than chance to have a third, and so on. I can't think of a type of 
social relationship I would anticipate this pattern for, but it could just 
be that I've never thought about the kind of relaitonship that you're 
studying, and it makes perfect sense to you. 

My other quesiton would be what your alpha is; that changes the fine 
quantitative details of the interpretation, but not the general 
qualitative interpretation. Unless your alpha is either essentially 0 or 
very very high, in which case it would change the latter as well. If it's 
in the 0.1 - 2.0 range, I don't think it would. 

I hope that helps! 
Steve

Hi Philip,

First, thanks for your patience.  This turned out to be a problem with many 
moving pieces, so it took a while to pin down each part.  And thanks for 
reporting this in the first place.

Second, I think we have basically good news to report:  your example revealed a 
couple of bugs (in both ergm 2.4 and 3.1), and a problem in your model, but the 
results you published were essentially correct.

In tracking down why your model didn't converge in 3.1, we ended up finding 4 
issues that contributed in different ways.  i'll list them in order of 
severity.

1. the unique naming problem

This was what prevented 3.1 from being able to fit your model at all (as Pavel 
correctly noted).  It's due to a change from 2.4 to 3.1 in the way variable 
names are used.  And while it's not clear that we want to encourage users to 
use the same name for two variables (in your case "weight"), ergm should detect 
and provide a warning rather than fail completely.  So this will be fixed.

As you and Pavel both noted, once you rename one of the offending variables, 
your model fits successfully and quickly in 3.1.  But, you don't get exactly 
the same results...

2. compression algorithm

There is an algorithm deep in ergm ("ergm.sufftoprob") that is intended to 
speed up computations, but was not written well.  It was called by default in 
2.4 (control=control.ergm(compress=T)), and is not called by default in 3.1 
(control=control.ergm(MCMC.compress=F)).  When it fails (as it did in your 
model), the result is that the SEs are often biased downward (as it was in your 
case).

Removing compression increases the size of the SEs.  Not enough to change the 
nominal significance levels for any of the coef you reported as significant, 
but enough to notice.


3. default fitting iterations

In 2.4, the default was 3 iterations, in 3.1 it has been raised to 20. If your 
model is difficult to fit or converges slowly (as it does in your case) more 
iterations can lead to different point estimates.

This is part of why the point estimates for your model are different in 3.1.


4. model issues:  colinearity

It turns out your model had a hidden colinearity problem.  The edges and gwesp 
statistic were nearly colinear (correlation above 0.99).  The reason is because 
you have a relatively dense network, so almost every edge is involved in at 
least one triangle.  Using a low alpha for gwesp (as you did) leads that 
statistic towards measuring how many edges are involved in at least one 
triangle (it is exactly that when alpha=0).  So each edge contributed the same 
amount to the change statistics for these two terms.

ergm 3.1 handles that colinearity better both because it has more fitting 
iterations, and because it doesn't use compression by default so the SEs are 
accurate.  so a default fit (with unique names) will show that edges and gwesp 
are highly correlated and the coef are not signficant.

But if you increase alpha (to, say, 1), you'll find that the colinearity is 
sufficiently reduced that the gwesp term becomes significant.  At this point, 
the gwDsp term is no longer significant.  You may find that changing the alpha 
for that term helps -- we left off here.


I've attached a spreadsheet that documents all of the models we fit to track 
down these different problems and verify what was causing what. There's a 
summary sheet up front that shows what matters substantively for your paper, 
and lots of stuff on the other two sheets to see the details.

I hope this helps -- let us know if you have any other questions.

best,
Martina, Dave and Steve

Megumi,

These value of alpha are not inherently problematic.  But you should be 
aware of the impact on the interpretation of the gwdsp term, and pay 
attention to the impact on the correlation between the gwdsp term and the

> On Thu, 6 Aug 2009, Jenine Harris wrote:
>
>
>> I was wondering if anyone has an example of how a GWDSP term would be
>
>> interpreted in somewhat lay terms. From my understanding GWDSP accounts for
>
>> the distribution of shared partnership for each dyad in a network, but I'm
>
>> not sure how to go about interpreting a negative signficant GWDSP
>
>> coefficient of -0.25 in an actual ERGM model. What does this say about the
>
>> distribution and how does it influence the likelihood of a tie?
>
>
>
> Hi Jenine,
>
> A great question. Yes, I do think GWDSP is a bit trickier than interpret
> than any of the other terms we commonly work with. I can give you my own
> idiosyncratic approach.
>
> First, as technical background: As you probably know, GWDSP is a
> parametric summary measure of the tendency for two actors to have x
> partners in common, regardless of whether the two actors themselves are
> tied. GWESP is the same measure, but only counted across two actors who
> are tied. The two are comparable to the "alternating 2-paths" and
> "alternating k-triangles" that Snijders et al discuss in a series of
> papers. The two measures, combined with a third (GW degree, or the
> comparable alternating k-stars) are derived in those papers by placing a
> parametric constraint on three sets of statistics that emerge when making
> a very sociologically reasonable set of assumptions about relational
> dependence. The three parametric stats are also seen to work well in
> practice at modeling real-world social networks and avoiding degeneracy
> when doing so.
>
> So, on to interpretation. As I said, I agree that GWDSP is the hardest to
> interpret. In fact, I personally never use a GWDSP term without also
> using a GWESP term. And once I combined the two, I always find that the
> GWDSP coefficient is close to zero, and non-significant. Let me see if I
> can give good intuition as to why.
>
> GWESP has some relatively clear interpetations (which I discuss in a few
> of my papers). In real-world data of friendship or collaboration or
> similar kinds of networks, it is generally significantly positive. This
> means that those who are tied are more likely than chance to have multiple
> shared partners.
>
> GWDSP tells whether shared partners tend to clump together, regardless of
> whether two people are tied or not. For example, whether or not you and I
> are friends, if we have one friend in common, are we more likely than
> expected by chance to have a second friend in common? And so on. If yes,
> the GWDSP coefficient will be positive. If it is zero, then we are as
> likely as chance to have one in common; if negative, then less.
>
> If one only uses GWDSP and not GWESP, then it's hard to know whether an
> observed non-random shared partner distribution is driven by pairs who are
> themselves tied, pairs who are not tied, or both. If you include both
> GWESP and GWDSP, then it becomes clear - GWDSP is the base effect (which
> now isolates the effect for those not tied only); GWESP occurs on top of
> this base, and isolates the effect for those who are tied. And what I
> have always found is that the GWESP effect is then strong and significant,
> and the GWDSP is tiny and insignificant. It may be that in different
> kinds of data GWDSP would be significant itself, though.
>
> My questions for you are: is your GWDSP term significant? Does it remain
> so when GWESP is added? If the answer to both questions is yes, then you
> have something particuarly interesting (and unprecendented, at least for
> me) on your hands. If it remains negative and significant, then that says
> that people who are not tied tend not to have multiple shared partners.
> Once two unconnected people have one shared partner, they're less likely
> than chance to have a second; if they do have a second, they're less
> likely than chance to have a third, and so on. I can't think of a type of
> social relationship I would anticipate this pattern for, but it could just
> be that I've never thought about the kind of relaitonship that you're
> studying, and it makes perfect sense to you.
>
> My other quesiton would be what your alpha is; that changes the fine
> quantitative details of the interpretation, but not the general
> qualitative interpretation. Unless your alpha is either essentially 0 or
> very very high, in which case it would change the latter as well. If it's
> in the 0.1 - 2.0 range, I don't think it would.
>
> I hope that helps!
> Steve
